questions.correctAnswer: The Pueblo peoples, including the Jumano
distractors: The Caddo
The Karankawa
The Comanche
questions.explanation: Pueblo peoples settled along the upper Rio Grande near present-day El Paso. They farmed irrigated fields and lived in multi-room adobe towns, while the Jumano among them also became famous traders.

img.scene: An adobe pueblo village of flat-roofed mud-brick houses beside a desert river in West Texas, farmers tending corn fields with irrigation channels, mountains behind, historical illustration.
img.tip: Pueblo peoples farmed the Rio Grande in adobe towns.
img.title: PUEBLO TOWNS OF WEST TEXAS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Pueblo homes were mud-brick apartments by the river.
questions.question: Which Native American peoples built settled farming towns of adobe houses along the upper Rio Grande in the Mountains and Basins region of West Texas?

questions.correctAnswer: They were skilled farmers who lived in the Piney Woods of East Texas
distractors: They were nomads who followed buffalo across the High Plains
They were fishers who traveled the Gulf Coast in dugout canoes
They were desert hunter-gatherers of the South Texas brush country
questions.explanation: The Caddo Confederacy farmed corn, beans, and squash in rich East Texas soil. Their villages had tall, beehive-shaped houses covered in grass thatch, led by chiefs and priests.

img.scene: An East Texas Native American village in a pine forest clearing with tall beehive-shaped thatched houses, people working corn fields, a ceremonial mound nearby, historical illustration.
img.tip: The Caddo farmed the Piney Woods in thatched villages.
img.title: THE CADDO OF EAST TEXAS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Caddo houses looked like giant beehives in the pines.
questions.question: Which statement best describes the Caddo people of Texas?

questions.correctAnswer: The Karankawa
distractors: The Caddo
The Jumano
The Wichita
questions.explanation: The Karankawa moved seasonally along the bays and barrier islands of the Gulf Coast. They fished and gathered shellfish, traveling between camps in dugout canoes.

img.scene: Native American coastal people fishing from dugout canoes in a calm Texas bay at sunrise, wading with nets and spears, a small camp of shelters on the shore, historical illustration.
img.tip: The Karankawa fished the bays from dugout canoes.
img.title: KARANKAWA OF THE GULF COAST

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Karankawa canoes cruised the coast for fish.
questions.question: Which Texas Native American group lived as nomadic fishers and hunters along the Gulf Coast, traveling in dugout canoes?

questions.correctAnswer: Food, hides for tipis and clothing, and bones for tools
distractors: Gold and silver for trading with Europeans
Cotton and tobacco for farming villages
Timber and stone for building permanent towns
questions.explanation: Plains peoples used nearly every part of the buffalo. Meat fed the band, hides became tipi covers, robes, and moccasins, and bones and horns were shaped into tools, cups, and weapons.

img.scene: A Plains Native American hunting camp with tipis, a large buffalo herd grazing on golden grassland in the distance, families working with hides stretched on frames, historical illustration.
img.tip: Plains peoples used almost every part of the buffalo.
img.title: THE BUFFALO PROVIDED ALMOST EVERYTHING

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: For Plains peoples, the buffalo was a walking supermarket.
questions.question: What did the buffalo provide for nomadic Plains peoples such as the Comanche and Apache?

questions.correctAnswer: They adapted their homes, food, and way of life to the land and resources of their own region
distractors: They all copied the culture of the Aztec Empire in Mexico
Their leaders met and divided Texas into four equal kingdoms
European explorers assigned each group a different way of life
questions.explanation: Texas has four natural regions with very different water, plants, and animals. Groups in each region built a culture around what their environment offered, from coastal fishing to desert farming.

img.scene: A four-part landscape panorama of Texas showing pine forests, a coastal bay, open grass plains, and desert mountains side by side under one sky, historical illustration.
img.tip: Different Texas lands produced different Native cultures.
img.title: FOUR REGIONS, FOUR WAYS OF LIFE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The land wrote the rules for each tribe's life.
questions.question: Why did Native American groups in Texas develop such different cultures from one another?

questions.correctAnswer: Corn, beans, and squash grown in farmed fields
distractors: Buffalo hunted on long seasonal migrations
Fish and shellfish gathered along the coast
Prickly pear and wild plants gathered in the desert
questions.explanation: Farming let groups like the Caddo and Pueblo stay in one place year-round. Surplus corn, beans, and squash supported larger, permanent villages with chiefs, priests, and craft workers.

img.scene: Native American farmers harvesting tall corn, beans, and squash in green fields beside a permanent village of sturdy houses, baskets of produce carried to storage, historical illustration.
img.tip: Farming corn, beans, and squash allowed permanent villages.
img.title: FARMING BUILT PERMANENT VILLAGES

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Corn, beans, and squash - the three sisters fed the villages.
questions.question: What food source allowed some Texas Native groups, such as the Caddo, to live in permanent villages instead of moving from place to place?

questions.correctAnswer: Coastal Karankawa fished from canoes while Plains groups followed buffalo herds
distractors: All Texas tribes built identical houses and ate the same foods
Texas tribes traded so much that their cultures became exactly alike
Spanish missionaries had already organized the tribes into towns
questions.explanation: A historian's claim needs matching evidence. Each group used what its region provided: seafood on the coast, buffalo on the plains, irrigated crops in the desert west, and farmed foods in the eastern forests.

img.scene: A split landscape view: on one side Native fishers in canoes on a coastal bay, on the other side mounted hunters following a buffalo herd across open plains, historical illustration.
img.tip: Canoes on the coast, buffalo on the plains - geography shaped culture.
img.title: EVIDENCE OF GEOGRAPHY AT WORK

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Match the tool to the territory - canoes here, buffalo there.
questions.question: A historian argues that geography shaped Texas Native American cultures. Which evidence best supports that claim?

questions.correctAnswer: Food and water were scarce in the dry brush country, so bands had to keep moving to survive
distractors: They were banned from farming by Spanish law
Their religion required them to visit every river in Texas each year
They were constantly fleeing the much larger Caddo Confederacy
questions.explanation: The Coahuiltecan peoples of South Texas survived on prickly pear fruit, mesquite beans, roots, and small game. With so little food in any one spot, small bands moved often and never grew large.

img.scene: A small band of Native hunter-gatherers walking through dry South Texas brush country with cactus and mesquite, carrying baskets and digging sticks, historical illustration.
img.tip: Scarce food and water kept Coahuiltecan bands small and moving.
img.title: SURVIVING THE BRUSH COUNTRY

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Little food, little water - so the Coahuiltecans kept walking.
questions.question: Why did Coahuiltecan bands in South Texas stay small and move frequently?

questions.correctAnswer: Alonso Alvarez de Pineda
distractors: Alvar Nunez Cabeza de Vaca
Francisco Vasquez de Coronado
Rene-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle
questions.explanation: In 1519 Pineda sailed the northern Gulf shore for Spain and drew the first European map of the Texas coast. His voyage showed that the land was one great continent, not islands or a passage to Asia.

img.scene: A Spanish sailing ship in 1519 exploring the Texas Gulf coastline, a navigator on deck drawing charts of the shore, calm green waters and sandy coast ahead, historical illustration.
img.tip: Pineda mapped the Texas coast in 1519.
img.title: 1519 - PINEDA MAPS THE COAST

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 1519 - Pineda penciled Texas onto the map.
questions.question: Which Spanish explorer mapped the Texas coast in 1519, producing the first European map of the Gulf of Mexico shoreline?

questions.correctAnswer: Near Galveston Island on the Texas coast
distractors: In the mountains of New Mexico
On the banks of the Mississippi River
Near present-day Dallas
questions.explanation: In 1528 a storm wrecked the rafts of the failed Narvaez expedition. Cabeza de Vaca and a few survivors washed ashore near Galveston Island and spent years traveling across Texas before reaching Mexico.

img.scene: Shipwrecked Spanish explorers in tattered clothes wading ashore from a broken raft onto a sandy Texas barrier island, waves and driftwood around them, historical illustration.
img.tip: Cabeza de Vaca washed ashore near Galveston Island in 1528.
img.title: SHIPWRECKED ON THE TEXAS COAST

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A shipwreck near Galveston started Cabeza de Vaca's long walk.
questions.question: Where was Alvar Nunez Cabeza de Vaca shipwrecked in 1528, beginning his years-long journey across Texas?

questions.correctAnswer: La Relacion, his account of Texas lands and peoples
distractors: The first printed map of the Pacific Ocean
A treaty between Spain and the Comanche
The charter founding the city of San Antonio
questions.explanation: Cabeza de Vaca wrote La Relacion after reaching Mexico in 1536. His descriptions of Texas geography, wildlife such as buffalo, and Native peoples gave Europeans their first real information about the region.

img.scene: A weary Spanish explorer in 16th-century dress writing in a large journal by candlelight, sketches of buffalo and prickly pear cactus on the pages, historical illustration.
img.tip: Cabeza de Vaca's La Relacion first described Texas to Europe.
img.title: LA RELACION - THE FIRST REPORT ON TEXAS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: He walked Texas, then wrote the book on it.
questions.question: What is Cabeza de Vaca best known for writing after his journey through Texas?

questions.correctAnswer: To find the rumored Seven Cities of Gold
distractors: To build a chain of missions along the Rio Grande
To sign a peace treaty with the Caddo Confederacy
To chart a river route to the Pacific Ocean
questions.explanation: Reports of wealthy cities to the north, fed by the friar Marcos de Niza, launched Coronado's expedition of 1540-1542. In the Texas Panhandle he found Plains peoples and buffalo herds, but no golden cities.

img.scene: A column of Spanish conquistadors in steel helmets and armor riding horses across a vast flat golden plain, a distant canyon rim on the horizon, historical illustration.
img.tip: Coronado chased golden cities and found plains instead.
img.title: CORONADO SEARCHES FOR GOLD

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Coronado hunted cities of gold and found oceans of grass.
questions.question: Why did Spain send Francisco Vasquez de Coronado into the Southwest and across the Texas plains in 1540?

questions.correctAnswer: Endless grasslands and huge buffalo herds, but no gold or wealthy cities
distractors: A rich silver mine guarded by Pueblo towns
A French trading post on the Gulf Coast
The golden city of Quivira, full of treasure
questions.explanation: Coronado crossed the Llano Estacado and saw Palo Duro Canyon and enormous buffalo herds. The expedition returned to Mexico having found no wealth, which cooled Spanish interest in Texas for generations.

img.scene: Spanish explorers on horseback looking over the rim of a great red-rock canyon filled with a sea of grazing buffalo below, wide plains stretching to the horizon, historical illustration.
img.tip: In the Panhandle Coronado found buffalo, not gold.
img.title: PALO DURO AND THE BUFFALO SEA

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No gold in Palo Duro - just a million buffalo.
questions.question: What did Coronado's expedition actually find when it crossed the Texas Panhandle?

questions.correctAnswer: France now claimed territory that Spain considered its own
distractors: The French fort blocked Spain's only port on the Gulf
La Salle had discovered the largest gold mine in Texas
The French settlers converted the Karankawa to Christianity
questions.explanation: La Salle claimed the Mississippi valley for France and built Fort St. Louis near Matagorda Bay in 1685. Alarmed, Spain searched for the fort and then planted missions in East Texas to hold the land.

img.scene: A rough wooden French fort with a flag flying beside a Texas coastal bay in 1685, settlers unloading supplies from a small ship, marshland and live oaks around, historical illustration.
img.tip: La Salle's French fort pushed Spain to occupy Texas.
img.title: LA SALLE AND FORT ST. LOUIS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A French flag on the coast woke Spain up fast.
questions.question: Why did La Salle's Fort St. Louis, built on the Texas coast in 1685, alarm Spanish officials?

questions.correctAnswer: European diseases such as smallpox, to which Native peoples had no immunity
distractors: Spanish laws that banned Native farming and hunting
A long drought that emptied Texas rivers for a century
Warfare between Texas tribes that began only after 1700
questions.explanation: Contact brought germs Native bodies had never met. Epidemics of smallpox and other diseases swept through villages repeatedly, killing far more people than battles did and weakening whole cultures.

img.scene: A quiet Native American village at dusk with empty houses and a medicine healer tending sick villagers wrapped in blankets, somber mood, historical illustration.
img.tip: Disease, not battle, caused the greatest Native losses.
img.title: THE SILENT KILLER - DISEASE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Invisible germs did what armies could not.
questions.question: Which consequence of European contact most reduced the Native American population of Texas?

questions.correctAnswer: Horses let hunters follow buffalo herds over long distances and turned groups like the Comanche into dominant powers
distractors: Horses replaced farming, so every Texas tribe became wealthy traders
Horses were used only for ceremonies and never for hunting or war
Horses made buffalo extinct within ten years of arriving
questions.explanation: Spanish horses escaped or were traded north and spread across the plains. Mounted hunters could travel farther, kill more buffalo, raid and trade over huge distances - a revolution that powered Comanche dominance for 150 years.

img.scene: Plains Native American riders on swift horses galloping alongside a running buffalo herd on open grassland, dust rising, hunting spears ready, historical illustration.
img.tip: Horses transformed Plains hunting, travel, and power.
img.title: THE HORSE CHANGES THE PLAINS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Give a hunter a horse and the whole plains shrink.
questions.question: Which statement best explains how the arrival of the horse changed life for Plains peoples in Texas?

questions.correctAnswer: Explorers found no gold or silver there, so Spain spent its energy on richer colonies
distractors: Texas law made it illegal for Spaniards to enter the region
The pope gave Texas to France in a treaty of 1550
Shipwrecks destroyed every Spanish fleet sent to Texas
questions.explanation: Coronado and others reported grass, buffalo, and resistant peoples - but no treasure. Spain focused on the silver of Mexico and Peru, and Texas stayed a neglected frontier until the French threat appeared in the 1680s.

img.scene: A dusty Spanish treasure caravan of mules loaded with silver leaving a rich Mexican mining town, while a faded map of an empty northern frontier lies forgotten on a table, historical illustration.
img.tip: No gold found - Spain ignored Texas for 150 years.
img.title: THE FORGOTTEN FRONTIER

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No glitter, no settlers - Spain looked the other way.
questions.question: Why did Spain largely ignore Texas for about 150 years after Coronado's expedition?

questions.explanation: In 1718 Spain founded Mission San Antonio de Valero - later famous as the Alamo - and the presidio of San Antonio de Bexar. San Antonio became the center of Spanish Texas and its most important town.

img.scene: Spanish friars and soldiers in 1718 raising the first wooden chapel and fort beside a spring-fed river in South Texas, Native workers helping, oak trees around, historical illustration.
img.tip: San Antonio was founded in 1718.
img.title: 1718 - SAN ANTONIO IS FOUNDED

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 1718 - San Antonio starts with a mission and a fort.
questions.question: In what year was San Antonio founded, with Mission San Antonio de Valero and its presidio, making it the heart of Spanish Texas?

questions.correctAnswer: To convert Native Americans to Christianity and make them loyal Spanish subjects
distractors: To serve as prisons for captured French soldiers
To mine gold and silver for the Spanish king
To grow cotton for export to Europe
questions.explanation: Friars gathered Native peoples into missions to teach them the Catholic faith, the Spanish language, and farming and trades. Missions were Spain's main tool for spreading its religion, culture, and control across the Texas frontier.

img.scene: A Spanish mission church of white stone with a bell tower, a friar teaching a group of Native American children in the courtyard, gardens and workshops nearby, historical illustration.
img.tip: Missions spread the Catholic faith and Spanish culture.
img.title: WHY SPAIN BUILT MISSIONS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A mission was a church, school, and farm in one.
questions.question: What was the main purpose of the Spanish missions built in Texas?

questions.correctAnswer: Military forts that protected the missions and settlements
distractors: Market towns where traders sold goods
Prisons for rebellious settlers
Rancho headquarters owned by wealthy families
questions.explanation: Presidios were forts staffed by Spanish soldiers. Placed near missions and towns, they guarded against raids, escorted travelers and supply trains, and carried out Spain's orders on the frontier.

img.scene: A square Spanish frontier fort of stone and adobe with a watchtower, soldiers on the walls and horses in the corral, a mission church visible in the distance, historical illustration.
img.tip: Presidios were the forts that guarded the missions.
img.title: PRESIDIOS - FRONTIER FORTS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Mission prayed, presidio protected - they came in pairs.
questions.question: What were the presidios in Spanish Texas?

questions.correctAnswer: They followed a daily routine of prayer, work in the fields and workshops, and learning Spanish customs
distractors: They lived freely outside the mission and visited only on holidays
They spent the day mining silver for the friars
They trained as soldiers to invade French Louisiana
questions.explanation: Mission bells set the schedule: worship, meals, farming, herding, weaving, and building. In exchange for food and protection, Native residents gave up much of their traditional life, and many died from European diseases in the crowded missions.

img.scene: Inside a Spanish mission compound at dawn, Native residents walking to fields with hoes while others weave cloth and tend cattle, a friar ringing the church bell, historical illustration.
img.tip: Mission life ran by the bell: prayer, work, and lessons.
img.title: A DAY INSIDE THE MISSION

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The mission bell ran the whole day.
questions.question: Which statement best describes daily life for Native Americans who lived inside a Spanish mission?

questions.correctAnswer: The royal road linking San Antonio and the East Texas missions with Mexico
distractors: A cattle trail from Texas to Kansas railheads
A river route used by French fur traders
The boundary line between Texas and Louisiana
questions.explanation: El Camino Real de los Tejas, the King's Highway, carried soldiers, supplies, mail, and settlers between Mexico City, San Antonio, and the missions near Louisiana. Parts of it are marked as a National Historic Trail today.

img.scene: A mule supply train and ox carts traveling a dusty royal road through Texas oak country toward a distant mission, soldiers riding escort, historical illustration.
img.tip: El Camino Real tied Texas missions to Mexico.
img.title: EL CAMINO REAL - THE KING'S HIGHWAY

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One royal road stitched Texas to Mexico.
questions.question: What was El Camino Real in Spanish Texas?

questions.correctAnswer: Settlers in Texas of Spanish or Mexican heritage, born or living in the region
distractors: Soldiers stationed at a presidio for a single year
Native peoples who had converted at a mission
French traders who crossed into Texas illegally
questions.explanation: Tejanos were the Spanish-speaking residents of Texas - ranchers, farmers, and townspeople from San Antonio to Nacogdoches. Their culture blended Spanish, Mexican, and frontier traditions and still shapes Texas today.

img.scene: A Spanish-speaking Texan ranching family in colonial dress outside an adobe home in San Antonio, cattle grazing nearby and a mission tower in the background, historical illustration.
img.tip: Tejanos were Texas settlers of Spanish-Mexican heritage.
img.title: THE TEJANOS OF SPANISH TEXAS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Tejanos - the first Texans of the Spanish frontier.
questions.question: Who were the Tejanos of the Spanish and Mexican eras?

questions.correctAnswer: Close most East Texas missions and presidios and pull the settlers back to San Antonio
distractors: Open Texas to unlimited immigration from the United States
Build a wall of forts along the Rio Grande
Move the capital of Texas to Nacogdoches
questions.explanation: After touring Texas in 1766-1768, the Marques de Rubi reported that the eastern settlements were costly, weak, and hard to defend. Spain followed his advice, and in 1773 East Texas settlers were ordered to San Antonio, though many later returned east.

img.scene: A Spanish inspector general in a fine uniform studying a large frontier map in a candlelit room, officers pointing at scattered missions marked across Texas, historical illustration.
img.tip: Rubi's report pulled East Texas settlers back to San Antonio.
img.title: THE MARQUES DE RUBI REPORT

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Rubi toured Texas and told Spain to shrink the map.
questions.question: What did the Marques de Rubi recommend after inspecting the Texas frontier in the 1760s?

questions.correctAnswer: The Caddo already had prosperous farms and French trade goods, so mission life offered them little
distractors: The Caddo had never met any Europeans before the friars arrived
Spain refused to build any churches in East Texas
The missions failed because Texas has no rivers in the east
questions.explanation: Unlike groups with fewer resources, the Caddo grew their own food surpluses and obtained French guns and goods through trade. Disease and pressure to abandon their customs made missions like Los Adaes hard to sustain.

img.scene: A small Spanish mission chapel standing nearly empty at the edge of a pine forest while a busy Caddo trading village with full corn cribs bustles in the distance, historical illustration.
img.tip: Prosperous Caddo had little reason to join a mission.
img.title: WHY EAST TEXAS MISSIONS STRUGGLED

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Full granaries and French goods beat mission bells.
questions.question: Why did Spain's missions among the Caddo in East Texas struggle to succeed?

questions.correctAnswer: The Battle of Medina
distractors: The Battle of San Jacinto
The Battle of Gonzales
The Battle of Palo Alto
questions.explanation: In 1813 the Republican Army of the North, joined by Anglo volunteers under Augustus Magee and led by Jose Bernardo Gutierrez de Lara, marched for independence from Spain. Royalist forces crushed it near the Medina River, and harsh reprisals followed in San Antonio.

img.scene: A chaotic 1813 battlefield on open South Texas prairie with royalist cavalry charging a line of republican volunteers, dust, fallen flags, and thick oak trees in the distance, historical illustration.
img.tip: Medina in 1813 is the bloodiest battle in Texas history.
img.title: THE BLOODIEST BATTLE - MEDINA, 1813

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Medina, 1813 - the fight Texas history cannot forget.
questions.question: Which battle of 1813, fought during the Gutierrez-Magee expedition's revolt against Spain, is considered the bloodiest battle ever fought on Texas soil?

questions.correctAnswer: Distance from Mexico's centers of power, raids by Comanche and Apache, and few chances to get rich kept settlers away
distractors: Spain charged settlers a fee of one thousand pesos to enter Texas
Texas land was reserved only for the Spanish royal family
Settlers were waiting for railroads to be built first
questions.explanation: After a century of colonization, Spanish Texas held only a few thousand settlers. Supplies traveled slowly over El Camino Real, frontier raids made farming dangerous, and with no gold or silver, few Spaniards chose the risk.

img.scene: A lonely Spanish frontier settlement of a few adobe houses and a mission beside miles of empty grassland, a distant dust trail of raiders on the horizon, vast sky, historical illustration.
img.tip: Danger, distance, and no riches kept Spanish Texas nearly empty.
img.title: A NEARLY EMPTY FRONTIER

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Far, dangerous, and poor - no wonder few came.
questions.question: Why did so few settlers live in Spanish Texas even after a hundred years of missions and presidios?

questions.explanation: Mexico won its independence from Spain in 1821 after an eleven-year struggle. Texas, still a sparsely settled northern frontier, became part of the new Mexican nation.

img.scene: A celebration in a Mexican town plaza in 1821 with people cheering under green, white, and red banners, church bells ringing and soldiers presenting arms, historical illustration.
img.tip: Mexico won independence from Spain in 1821.
img.title: 1821 - MEXICAN INDEPENDENCE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 1821 - Texas trades a Spanish flag for a Mexican one.
questions.question: In what year did Mexico win independence from Spain, making Texas part of Mexico?

questions.correctAnswer: An agent hired to bring settlers into Texas in exchange for land
distractors: The commander of a Mexican army unit
A Native American tribal chief
A Spanish missionary priest
questions.explanation: Under colonization laws, empresarios received large land grants and earned bonus land for each family they settled. Stephen F. Austin became the most successful empresario, but dozens of others signed contracts.

img.scene: A land agent in 1820s frontier dress showing a large parchment land grant to a family of settlers beside their covered wagon on the Texas prairie, historical illustration.
img.tip: An empresario traded settlers for land grants.
img.title: WHAT IS AN EMPRESARIO?

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Empresario - bring families, earn land.
questions.question: What was an empresario in Mexican Texas?

questions.correctAnswer: Stephen F. Austin
distractors: Sam Houston
Moses Austin
Green DeWitt
questions.explanation: Stephen F. Austin carried out the grant his father Moses had received and founded Austin's Colony, bringing the first 300 Anglo families, called the Old Three Hundred, in the 1820s. His success earned him the title Father of Texas.

img.scene: A young 1820s colony leader greeting arriving settler families with wagons along a Texas river, surveying land with a compass and chain, new cabins rising behind, historical illustration.
img.tip: Stephen F. Austin founded the first Anglo colony in Texas.
img.title: STEPHEN F. AUSTIN - FATHER OF TEXAS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Austin brought the Old Three Hundred home to Texas.
questions.question: Who is known as the Father of Texas for founding the first successful Anglo American colony there in the 1820s?

questions.correctAnswer: It made Mexico a federal republic, and Texas was joined with Coahuila as one state
distractors: It gave Texas complete independence from Mexico
It made the Mexican president a king for life
It banned all immigration from the United States
questions.explanation: The Constitution of 1824 modeled Mexico partly on the United States, with power shared between national and state governments. Texas lacked the population to be its own state, so it merged with Coahuila as Coahuila y Tejas, with the capital far away at Saltillo.

img.scene: Mexican lawmakers in 1824 gathered around a table signing a large constitution document in a grand hall, candles and national banners around them, historical illustration.
img.tip: The 1824 constitution made Texas part of Coahuila y Tejas.
img.title: THE CONSTITUTION OF 1824

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 1824 - a federal Mexico, and Texas tied to Coahuila.
questions.question: What did Mexico's Constitution of 1824 do that shaped Texas government?

questions.correctAnswer: To develop the land's economy and create a settled population that could guard the frontier
distractors: To find soldiers for Mexico's war with Spain
To punish Anglo Americans by moving them far away
To convert Texans to the Catholic faith
questions.explanation: Texas was rich in land but nearly empty. Mexican leaders hoped immigrant farmers would raise crops and cattle, pay taxes, and form a human buffer against Native raids and foreign invasion on the northern frontier.

img.scene: Immigrant settler families arriving with wagons and livestock at a green Texas river crossing, surveyors marking farm plots on the open land, historical illustration.
img.tip: Mexico wanted settlers to grow the economy and hold the frontier.
img.title: WHY MEXICO INVITED SETTLERS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Mexico needed farmers as a living fence on the frontier.
questions.question: Why did Mexico invite settlers from the United States to colonize Texas?

questions.correctAnswer: Become Mexican citizens and accept the Catholic Church, Mexico's official religion
distractors: Serve two years in the Mexican army
Pay half of every harvest to the empresario
Give up speaking English in their homes
questions.explanation: Colonization laws demanded loyalty to Mexico, good moral character, and support of the Catholic faith. Many Anglo settlers agreed on paper but kept their own language, customs, and Protestant faith in practice, which fed future tension.

img.scene: Settler families signing colonization papers at a wooden table in a Mexican land office, an official with a large registry book and a priest standing nearby, historical illustration.
img.tip: Settlers pledged loyalty to Mexico and the Catholic faith.
img.title: THE PRICE OF MEXICAN LAND

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sign here: citizen of Mexico, Catholic on paper.
questions.question: What did Anglo settlers promise when they received land in Mexican Texas?

questions.correctAnswer: The Fredonian Rebellion at Nacogdoches
distractors: The Battle of Gonzales
The Turtle Bayou Resolutions
The Mier y Teran Report
questions.explanation: Empresario Haden Edwards clashed with older settlers and Mexican officials over land titles. In December 1826 his followers seized Nacogdoches and declared the Republic of Fredonia. The revolt collapsed quickly, but it frightened Mexico into watching Texas closely.

img.scene: A small group of rebels raising a homemade banner over the stone Old Stone Fort building in Nacogdoches in winter 1826, armed settlers gathering in the street, historical illustration.
img.tip: The Fredonian Rebellion was the first Anglo revolt in Texas.
img.title: THE FREDONIAN REBELLION, 1826

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Fredonia flared and fizzled, but Mexico took notice.
questions.question: Which event of 1826 - an empresario's short-lived revolt near Nacogdoches - first raised Mexican fears about Anglo settlers in Texas?

questions.correctAnswer: Mexican officials feared the United States was gaining too much influence in Texas
distractors: Texas had run out of land to grant new settlers
The Mexican president wanted Texas land for his own ranch
Anglo settlers had asked Mexico to close the border
questions.explanation: After inspecting Texas, General Manuel de Mier y Teran warned that Anglo settlers outnumbered Mexicans ten to one and still lived like Americans. The Law of April 6, 1830 banned further immigration from the United States, canceled unfinished empresario contracts, and taxed imports.

img.scene: A Mexican general in uniform writing a serious report by lantern light in a frontier camp, stacks of maps and census lists on the table beside him, historical illustration.
img.tip: Mier y Teran's warning produced the Law of April 6, 1830.
img.title: THE LAW OF APRIL 6, 1830

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Ten Anglos for every Mexican - Teran slammed the door.
questions.question: Mexico passed the Law of April 6, 1830, which banned further immigration from the United States, mainly because -

questions.correctAnswer: They still saw themselves as loyal Mexicans defending the federal Constitution of 1824
distractors: They had already declared Texas an independent republic
They invited the United States to annex Texas immediately
They demanded that Santa Anna be removed by the Texan army
questions.explanation: When Mexican troops arrested settlers at Anahuac in 1832, colonists at Turtle Bayou blamed the centralist government of Bustamante and declared support for Santa Anna, who was then fighting as a federalist. Loyalty to Mexico had not yet turned into revolution.

img.scene: Texas colonists in 1832 gathered around a table in a cabin drafting resolutions by candlelight, writing materials and a copy of a constitution on the table, historical illustration.
img.tip: In 1832 Texans still defended Mexico's 1824 constitution.
img.title: THE TURTLE BAYOU RESOLUTIONS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 1832 - rebels for the constitution, not yet for independence.
questions.question: What did the Turtle Bayou Resolutions of 1832 reveal about how many Texas colonists still viewed their relationship with Mexico?

questions.correctAnswer: He set aside the Constitution of 1824 and took power away from the states
distractors: He lowered taxes on Texas imports
He gave Texas its own separate state government
He moved the capital of Mexico to San Antonio
questions.explanation: Santa Anna won power as a federalist but ruled as a centralist, dissolving Congress and state legislatures and crushing resistance in Zacatecas. Texans who had settled under the federal Constitution of 1824 saw their self-government disappear, and many concluded only independence would protect it.

img.scene: A stern Mexican president-general in a decorated uniform tearing up a large constitution document before an assembly hall, alarmed lawmakers looking on, historical illustration.
img.tip: Santa Anna's centralism killed the self-government Texans expected.
img.title: SANTA ANNA TURNS CENTRALIST

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Rip up 1824, and Texas starts thinking revolution.
questions.question: How did Santa Anna's shift to centralist rule push Texas toward revolution?

questions.correctAnswer: Gonzales, over a small cannon marked by the 'Come and Take It' flag
distractors: The Alamo, over control of San Antonio
Goliad, over a shipment of rifles
San Jacinto, over the surrender of Santa Anna
questions.explanation: In October 1835 Mexican soldiers came to Gonzales to reclaim a small cannon given for defense against raids. Texans refused, raised a flag daring the soldiers to 'Come and Take It,' and fired the first shots of the Texas Revolution.

img.scene: Texas settlers in 1835 defending a small brass cannon in a dusty town street, a white homemade banner flying above them, Mexican soldiers approaching in the distance, historical illustration.
img.tip: The Revolution began at Gonzales over one small cannon.
img.title: COME AND TAKE IT - GONZALES, 1835

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One little cannon, one big dare: come and take it.
questions.question: Where did the Texas Revolution begin in October 1835, and what sparked the fight?

questions.correctAnswer: William B. Travis
distractors: James Bowie
Sam Houston
Stephen F. Austin
questions.explanation: Lt. Col. William Barret Travis commanded the Alamo garrison. His famous letter 'To the People of Texas and All Americans in the World' asked for reinforcements and promised 'Victory or Death.' He died in the final assault on March 6, 1836.

img.scene: A young Texan officer writing a letter by candlelight inside a mission room at night, his sword and papers on the desk, a worried expression, historical illustration.
img.tip: Travis commanded the Alamo and wrote for help.
img.title: TRAVIS AND THE ALAMO LETTER

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Travis signed it 'Victory or Death' - and meant it.
questions.question: Who commanded the Texas forces defending the Alamo in 1836?

questions.correctAnswer: San Jacinto, where Texans defeated Santa Anna's army in about 18 minutes
distractors: The Alamo, where Texans held out for thirteen days
Gonzales, where the first shots were fired
Washington-on-the-Brazos, where independence was declared
questions.explanation: On April 21, 1836, Sam Houston's army surprised Santa Anna's camp during its afternoon rest near the San Jacinto River. The battle lasted about 18 minutes and won Texas its independence.

img.scene: Texan soldiers charging across a grassy battlefield beside a wide river at golden afternoon light, smoke rising, an enemy camp in confusion ahead of them, historical illustration.
img.tip: San Jacinto won independence in about 18 minutes.
img.title: SAN JACINTO - 18 MINUTES TO VICTORY

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Eighteen minutes at San Jacinto changed Texas forever.
questions.question: Which battle on April 21, 1836 won Texas its independence from Mexico?

questions.correctAnswer: March 2, 1836, at Washington-on-the-Brazos
distractors: October 2, 1835, at Gonzales
April 21, 1836, at San Jacinto
December 29, 1845, at Austin
questions.explanation: While the Alamo was under siege, delegates at Washington-on-the-Brazos adopted the Texas Declaration of Independence on March 2, 1836 and created a government for the new Republic of Texas. March 2 is still celebrated as Texas Independence Day.

img.scene: Delegates in 1836 frontier dress signing a large declaration document inside a plain unfinished wooden building, cold light through the windows, historical illustration.
img.tip: Texas declared independence on March 2, 1836.
img.title: TEXAS INDEPENDENCE DAY - MARCH 2

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: March 2 - Texas writes itself a birthday.
questions.question: When and where did Texas declare independence from Mexico?

questions.correctAnswer: 'Remember the Alamo! Remember Goliad!'
distractors: 'Come and Take It!'
'Victory or Death!'
'Liberty or Death!'
questions.explanation: Houston's men charged shouting the names of the two disasters of March 1836. The Alamo's fall and the execution of Fannin's men at Goliad had turned grief and anger into the Revolution's most powerful motivation.

img.scene: Texan soldiers surging forward in a battle charge across open grass, shouting with raised rifles and flags, smoke and late-afternoon sun behind them, historical illustration.
img.tip: San Jacinto's cry honored the Alamo and Goliad dead.
img.title: THE BATTLE CRY AT SAN JACINTO

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two names shouted at San Jacinto: Alamo and Goliad.
questions.question: What battle cry did Sam Houston's soldiers shout as they charged at San Jacinto?

questions.correctAnswer: Colonel James Fannin and more than 300 of his men were executed after surrendering
distractors: Texans won a surprise victory over Santa Anna's main army
The Texas Declaration of Independence was signed there
Mexican forces abandoned Texas and returned home
questions.explanation: After surrendering at Coleto Creek, Fannin and his men were held at Goliad. On Palm Sunday, March 27, 1836, Mexican troops marched out more than 300 prisoners and shot them, following Santa Anna's orders to execute captured rebels.

img.scene: A somber view of the old Spanish presidio fortress at Goliad at dawn with flags lowered, mourning townspeople in the distance, historical illustration.
img.tip: At Goliad, surrendered Texans were executed in 1836.
img.title: THE GOLIAD MASSACRE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Goliad's prisoners never came home - Texas remembered.
questions.question: What happened at Goliad in March 1836?

questions.correctAnswer: The flight of Texas civilians eastward ahead of Santa Anna's advancing army
distractors: The retreat of the Mexican army after San Jacinto
A cattle drive from Texas to Louisiana
The march of Houston's army toward the Alamo
questions.explanation: After the Alamo fell and Goliad's men were executed, terrified families grabbed what they could carry and fled toward Louisiana, abandoning homes in the rain and mud. The Runaway Scrape ended with the victory at San Jacinto.

img.scene: Frightened settler families fleeing on muddy roads in the rain with wagons, children, and a few belongings, dark smoke on the horizon behind them, historical illustration.
img.tip: The Runaway Scrape was the civilians' flight in 1836.
img.title: THE RUNAWAY SCRAPE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Families ran east through the mud - the Runaway Scrape.
questions.question: What was the Runaway Scrape during the Texas Revolution?

questions.correctAnswer: To gain time to train his small army and draw Santa Anna farther from his supplies
distractors: He was secretly planning to surrender to Mexico
He hoped the United States army would arrive and fight for Texas
He was lost and could not find Santa Anna's army
questions.explanation: Houston's raw volunteers were no match for Santa Anna at first. By retreating, Houston trained his men, gathered supplies, and stretched the Mexican supply lines thin until he could attack at a place and moment of his choosing - San Jacinto.

img.scene: A Texan army column marching east through pine woods, its general on horseback looking back thoughtfully over his shoulder at distant dust clouds, historical illustration.
img.tip: Houston retreated to train his army and pick his moment.
img.title: HOUSTON'S STRATEGIC RETREAT

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Houston backed up to load the spring - then struck.
questions.question: Why did Sam Houston keep retreating eastward instead of fighting Santa Anna right away?

questions.correctAnswer: End the war, withdraw Mexican troops from Texas, and work toward recognizing Texas independence
distractors: Give Texas back to Spain in exchange for peace
Pay Texas ten million dollars in gold
Join Texas as a general in the Mexican army
questions.explanation: Captured after San Jacinto, Santa Anna signed two treaties at Velasco, one public and one secret, in May 1836. Mexico's government later refused to accept them because they were signed by a prisoner, leaving the border unsettled for years.

img.scene: A captured Mexican general in a worn uniform signing documents at a rough table in a Texan camp, Texan officers standing watch around him, historical illustration.
img.tip: At Velasco, Santa Anna promised to end the war.
img.title: THE TREATIES OF VELASCO

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A captured general's signature bought Texas its breathing room.
questions.question: What did Santa Anna agree to in the Treaties of Velasco in 1836?

questions.correctAnswer: He set aside public land to fund public schools and universities
distractors: He built the first railroad across Texas
He founded the city of Houston as the capital
He paid off the entire national debt in one year
questions.explanation: President Mirabeau B. Lamar believed education would secure the Republic's future. His government reserved land in every county for schools and for two universities, an endowment that later helped create Texas public education.

img.scene: A 19th-century Texas president in formal dress signing land documents at a desk stacked with school land grants, a map of counties on the wall behind him, historical illustration.
img.tip: Lamar funded future schools with public land.
img.title: LAMAR - FATHER OF TEXAS EDUCATION

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Lamar banked land for schools not yet built.
questions.question: Why is Republic president Mirabeau B. Lamar called the Father of Texas Education?

questions.correctAnswer: Sending the Santa Fe Expedition to claim territory in New Mexico
distractors: Cutting the military budget to save money
Making peace treaties with the Comanche
Asking the United States for annexation right away
questions.explanation: Lamar expanded where Houston had retrenched. His 1841 Santa Fe Expedition tried to claim New Mexico for Texas but ended with the Texans captured and marched to Mexico City. Lamar also moved the capital to Austin and forced the Cherokee out of East Texas.

img.scene: An exhausted wagon expedition of Texans struggling across a dry desert plain in 1841, empty water barrels and weary oxen under a blazing sun, historical illustration.
img.tip: Lamar's Santa Fe Expedition failed in the desert.
img.title: THE SANTA FE EXPEDITION, 1841

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Lamar reached for Santa Fe and grabbed a disaster.
questions.question: Which action belonged to Lamar's expansion policy rather than Houston's cautious one?

questions.correctAnswer: Northern states opposed adding another slave state, and many Americans feared war with Mexico
distractors: Texas refused every offer of annexation from Washington
The United States could not afford the train fare for negotiators
Mexico offered Texas more money than the United States could
questions.explanation: Annexing a huge slaveholding republic threatened the balance between free and slave states in the U.S. Senate. Mexico also warned that annexation meant war. Texas waited nearly ten years before joining the Union in 1845.

img.scene: American lawmakers in the 1840s arguing heatedly in a grand congressional hall, a large map showing Texas hanging on the wall behind the speaker, historical illustration.
img.tip: Slavery politics and fear of war delayed annexation.
img.title: WHY ANNEXATION WAITED

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A slave-state Texas stalled in Washington for nine years.
questions.question: What was a major reason the United States delayed annexing Texas after 1836?

questions.correctAnswer: A massive public debt and paper money that lost almost all its value
distractors: A population so large that farmland ran out
An invasion by the French army
Earthquakes that destroyed the capital twice
questions.explanation: The Republic borrowed heavily for its army and navy and printed paper 'redbacks' that sank to a few cents on the dollar. By 1845 Texas owed roughly ten million dollars, one reason annexation by the United States looked attractive.

img.scene: A worried Republic-era shopkeeper examining nearly worthless red paper banknotes by lamplight, stacks of unpaid bills on the counter of his frontier store, historical illustration.
img.tip: Debt and worthless redbacks weakened the Republic.
img.title: THE BROKE REPUBLIC

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Redbacks worth pennies - the Republic was broke.
questions.question: Which problem most weakened the Republic of Texas during its ten years as a nation?

questions.correctAnswer: Anson Jones
distractors: Sam Houston
J. Pinckney Henderson
Mirabeau B. Lamar
questions.explanation: Anson Jones, the Republic's last president, managed the final negotiations and lowered the Texas flag at the annexation ceremony in 1846. J. Pinckney Henderson then became the first governor of the State of Texas.

img.scene: A solemn 1846 ceremony outside a Texas government building as the Lone Star flag is lowered on a pole, officials in formal dress and a crowd watching, historical illustration.
img.tip: Anson Jones was the Republic's last president.
img.title: THE LAST PRESIDENT OF THE REPUBLIC

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Jones lowered the Lone Star; statehood raised the Stars and Stripes.
questions.question: Who was president of the Republic of Texas when annexation to the United States was completed?

questions.correctAnswer: The Law of April 6, 1830; the Battle of Gonzales; the fall of the Alamo; the victory at San Jacinto
distractors: The fall of the Alamo; the Law of April 6, 1830; the Battle of Gonzales; the victory at San Jacinto
The Battle of Gonzales; the victory at San Jacinto; the Law of April 6, 1830; the fall of the Alamo
The victory at San Jacinto; the fall of the Alamo; the Battle of Gonzales; the Law of April 6, 1830
questions.explanation: Tensions built from Mexico's 1830 immigration ban to the first shots at Gonzales in October 1835. The Alamo fell in March 1836, and Houston's victory at San Jacinto followed on April 21, 1836.

img.scene: A sweeping Texas Revolution panorama: a small cannon and town on the left, a mission church in the center, and a river battlefield at sunset on the right, historical illustration.
img.tip: 1830 ban, Gonzales, the Alamo, then San Jacinto.
img.title: THE ROAD TO INDEPENDENCE IN ORDER

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Ban, cannon, Alamo, victory - in that order.
questions.question: Which sequence lists these events of the Texas Revolution era in the correct order?

questions.explanation: After years of debate, the United States Congress approved annexation and Texas voters accepted it. Texas entered the Union on December 29, 1845, as the 28th state.

img.scene: A celebration in 1845 Texas with the United States flag rising on a tall pole as crowds in frontier dress cheer, wagons and a courthouse behind them, historical illustration.
img.tip: Texas became the 28th state in 1845.
img.title: 1845 - TEXAS JOINS THE UNION

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 1845 - the 28th star joins the flag.
questions.question: In what year did Texas become a state in the United States?

questions.correctAnswer: A border dispute - the United States claimed the Rio Grande, while Mexico claimed the Nueces River
distractors: A fight over who owned the port of Galveston
Mexico's invasion of California
A disagreement about the price of cotton
questions.explanation: Texas had claimed the Rio Grande as its southern border since 1836, but Mexico insisted the border was the Nueces River, about 150 miles northeast. When U.S. troops entered the disputed strip in 1846, fighting broke out and war followed.

img.scene: Two lines of soldiers facing each other across a brushy river valley in South Texas in 1846, flags raised on both banks, tense stillness, historical illustration.
img.tip: The war started over two different claimed rivers.
img.title: TWO RIVERS, ONE BORDER DISPUTE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Rio Grande or Nueces? That argument started a war.
questions.question: What disagreement directly led to the Mexican-American War in 1846?

questions.correctAnswer: Texas gave up its claims to land in present-day New Mexico, Colorado, and beyond, and the United States paid Texas $10 million for its debts
distractors: Texas sold the Alamo to the United States Army for $10 million
The United States gave Texas all of New Mexico in exchange for Galveston
Texas agreed to end slavery in exchange for new railroads
questions.explanation: The young state of Texas claimed a huge wedge of the West reaching to Santa Fe and beyond. In the Compromise of 1850, Texas accepted its present-day boundaries and used the federal payment to finally pay off the old Republic's debts.

img.scene: Officials in 1850 studying a large map of Texas whose western boundary is being redrawn with a ruler and ink, stacks of debt papers on the desk, historical illustration.
img.tip: The Compromise of 1850 set Texas's present borders.
img.title: THE COMPROMISE OF 1850

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Texas traded far-off claims for cash to pay its debts.
questions.question: What did the Compromise of 1850 settle between Texas and the United States?

questions.correctAnswer: Near Brownsville in South Texas, at Palo Alto and Resaca de la Palma
distractors: At the Alamo in San Antonio
Along the Sabine River in East Texas
At El Paso in far West Texas
questions.explanation: General Zachary Taylor's army met Mexican forces in the brush country north of the Rio Grande in May 1846. The battles of Palo Alto and Resaca de la Palma, the war's first major fights, were U.S. victories.

img.scene: American artillery firing across a palm-dotted South Texas prairie in 1846, soldiers advancing through chaparral brush, smoke drifting over the field, historical illustration.
img.tip: The war's first battles were fought near Brownsville.
img.title: FIRST BLOOD - PALO ALTO, 1846

questions.correctAnswer: A German colonization society recruited them and founded towns such as New Braunfels and Fredericksburg
distractors: The Mexican government forced them to move to Texas
They were soldiers left over from the Texas Revolution
They came to work in the Spindletop oil fields
questions.explanation: The Adelsverein, a society of German nobles, promoted emigration to Texas in the 1840s. Thousands of German families crossed the Atlantic for land and opportunity, founding New Braunfels in 1845 and Fredericksburg in 1846 and leaving a lasting German mark on the Hill Country.

img.scene: German immigrant families in 1840s dress arriving with wagons at a new Hill Country town site, stone houses being built beside a clear creek, limestone hills behind, historical illustration.
img.tip: German societies founded New Braunfels and Fredericksburg.
img.title: GERMANS IN THE HILL COUNTRY

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: New Braunfels, 1845 - Germany plants roots in Texas.
questions.question: Why did thousands of German immigrants settle in the Texas Hill Country in the 1840s?

questions.correctAnswer: Americans believed it was their nation's destiny to expand westward across the continent
distractors: The United States wanted Texas mainly as a prison colony
Mexico asked the United States to take Texas off its hands
Texas had discovered the largest gold deposit in North America
questions.explanation: Manifest Destiny was the popular idea that the United States was meant to stretch from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Annexing Texas in 1845, then gaining the Southwest in the Mexican-American War, fulfilled much of that vision within a few years.

img.scene: Settler wagon trains rolling west across a vast prairie toward a setting sun, a huge American flag flying over a frontier town in the foreground, historical illustration.
img.tip: Manifest Destiny framed expansion as America's fate.
img.title: MANIFEST DESTINY MOVES WEST

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sea to shining sea - that slogan pulled Texas in.
questions.question: How did the annexation of Texas reflect the idea of Manifest Destiny?

questions.correctAnswer: Texas kept control of its public lands and kept the right to divide into as many as five states
distractors: Texas was allowed to keep its own army and navy forever
Texas could leave the Union whenever its legislature voted to
Texas paid no federal taxes for the first fifty years
questions.explanation: Unlike other states, Texas entered the Union owning its unappropriated public lands, which later funded schools and universities. The 1845 annexation terms also allowed Texas to split into up to five states, a right that still exists in theory.

img.scene: Surveyors in 1845 measuring vast open Texas grasslands with chains and a compass, a government official recording the public lands in a large ledger, historical illustration.
img.tip: Texas kept its public lands - and a five-state option.
img.title: TEXAS'S UNUSUAL ANNEXATION TERMS

questions.correctAnswer: The Confederate States of America
distractors: The Republic of Texas, restored as a nation
Mexico
The United States of America as a territory
questions.explanation: In February 1861 a Texas convention voted to secede, and voters approved it. Governor Sam Houston warned against the move but could not stop it. Texas joined the Confederacy and sent tens of thousands of soldiers to the Civil War.

img.scene: A large crowd in 1861 outside a Texas courthouse as delegates announce secession, a Confederate flag being raised while an elderly governor watches grimly, historical illustration.
img.tip: Texas seceded in 1861 and joined the Confederacy.
img.title: 1861 - TEXAS SECEDES

questions.correctAnswer: He refused to take an oath of allegiance to the Confederacy
distractors: He lost a statewide election by three votes
He moved to Mexico to live in exile
He was captured by Union soldiers at Galveston
questions.explanation: Sam Houston, the hero of San Jacinto, believed secession would bring ruin. When he would not swear allegiance to the Confederate States, the secession convention declared his office vacant in March 1861.

img.scene: An elderly statesman in a plain dark suit standing alone and resolute in a legislative hall as officials turn away from him, papers scattered on the desk, historical illustration.
img.tip: Houston refused the Confederate oath and lost his office.
img.title: HOUSTON REFUSES THE OATH

distractors: Texas voted to rejoin the United States
The last Confederate general surrendered at Appomattox
The port of Galveston was opened to world trade
questions.explanation: On June 19, 1865, U.S. General Gordon Granger arrived in Galveston and announced that enslaved people in Texas were free under the Emancipation Proclamation. African Americans in Texas marked the day as Juneteenth, now a federal holiday.

img.scene: Newly freed African American families celebrating joyfully in a Galveston street in June 1865 as a Union officer reads a proclamation from a balcony, historical illustration.
img.tip: Juneteenth, June 19, 1865, brought freedom news to Texas.
img.title: JUNETEENTH - FREEDOM COMES TO TEXAS

distractors: To win independence for Texas as its own nation again
To stop Mexico from invading Texas
To protest the building of railroads by Northern companies
questions.explanation: By 1860 about 30 percent of Texans were enslaved, and cotton grown by enslaved labor was the state's great money crop. Secession leaders argued states' rights mainly to defend the institution of slavery from a federal government they feared would end it.

img.scene: Enslaved workers picking cotton in a vast Texas field in 1860 under a hot sun, bales stacked on a wagon beside a plantation house, historical illustration.
img.tip: Cotton and slavery stood at the center of secession.
img.title: WHY TEXAS SECEDED

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Follow the cotton money and you find secession's cause.

distractors: Its navy defeated the Union blockade at New Orleans
Its capital hosted the Confederate government for two years
Its factories produced most of the Confederacy's rifles
questions.explanation: More than 70,000 Texans served in the Confederate military, in units like Hood's Texas Brigade. At home, wagon trains hauled cotton to Matamoros in neutral Mexico, dodging the Union blockade to exchange cotton for guns, medicine, and goods.

img.scene: Long wagon trains loaded with cotton bales rolling across a dusty South Texas road toward a river port, teamsters and armed escorts alongside, historical illustration.
img.tip: Texas sent soldiers east and cotton south through Mexico.
img.title: TEXAS FEEDS THE CONFEDERACY

distractors: Union forces captured the city and held it for the rest of the war
The city was destroyed by a hurricane during the battle
Texas troops surrendered the city without firing a shot

img.scene: Steamboats armored with cotton bales exchanging fire with warships in a harbor at dawn in 1863, soldiers storming the wharves of a port city, historical illustration.
img.tip: Cottonclads helped retake Galveston on New Year's Day 1863.

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Cotton bales as armor - Galveston was retaken by cottonclads.

distractors: It was the first battle of the Civil War
More soldiers fought there than at Gettysburg
It was the only battle fought entirely at sea

img.scene: A peaceful coastal Texas landscape at dawn with palm trees and brush beside a wide calm river, an empty grassy historic battlefield field in warm morning light, historical illustration.
img.tip: Palmito Ranch was fought after the war had already ended.
img.title: PALMITO RANCH - THE LAST BATTLE

distractors: They captured the city of Houston for the Union
They sank the entire Union navy in the Gulf of Mexico
They negotiated the peace treaty that ended the war in Texas

distractors: Texas was permanently divided into five military states
Slavery was re-established under a new name in the constitution
The governor was given lifetime powers by Congress
questions.explanation: Under the Reconstruction Acts, Texas was placed under military rule and had to write a new constitution guaranteeing Black male suffrage. In 1869 Texans elected African American legislators for the first time, though these gains were rolled back after Reconstruction ended.

distractors: The United States ordered Texas to weaken its government
Texans wanted to prepare to rejoin Mexico

img.scene: Delegates at a crowded 1875 Texas constitutional convention debating around long tables piled with papers and law books, gaslight and cigar smoke in the hall air, historical illustration.

distractors: They shipped cattle by steamboat down the Rio Grande
